An Albanese map for X is a pair (P, f) where P\rightarrow S$P\rightarrow S$ is a family of para-abelian varieties and f:X\rightarrow P$f:X\rightarrow P$ is a morphism satisfying the following condition: For each s\in S$s\in S$ the homomorphism f^*$f^*$ identifies {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{P/S}\otimes \kappa (s)${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{P/S}\otimes \kappa (s)$ with the maximal abelian subvariety of {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\otimes \kappa (s)${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\otimes \kappa (s)$. ... This follows from the fact that the maximal abelian subvarieties are stable under field extensions (Theorem 7.2). \square $\square $
The representability of the Picard functor was extended to arbitrary proper schemes by Murre (1964).

In the absence of rational points, however, notorious complications arise and Albanese maps take values in principal homogeneous spaces rather than abelian varieties. These problems become even more pronounced over imperfect fields of characteristic p>0$p>0$: To our best knowledge, the existence of Albanese map, and its base-change behavior, is only established for geometrically integral proper schemes, or more generally for geometrically reduced and geometrically connected proper schemes, compare the discussions of Conrad (2017) and Wittenberg (2008). Also see Achter et al. (2022) (formerly the appendix in the preprint Achter et al. 2019), and Schröer (xxx) for non-proper X.

After the completion of the present work, we learned that Albanese maps where also constructed in the setting of algebraic stacks by (Brochard 2021, Section 7 and 8). ### Theorem

(see Thm. 10.2) Assumptions as above. If {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$ admits a family of maximal abelian subvarieties, then there is an Albanese map f:X\rightarrow {\text {Alb}}_{X/S}$f:X\rightarrow {\text {Alb}}_{X/S}$. Moreover, it is universal for morphisms into families of para-abelian varieties, equivariant with respect to actions of group spaces, and commutes with base-change.

If the base scheme S is integral, and the generic fiber of {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\rightarrow S${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\rightarrow S$ is proper, all assumptions are satisfied at least on some dense open set U, over which the Albanese map thus exists. If S is the spectrum of a field k we get for each proper algebraic space X with h^0(\mathscr {O}_X)=1$h^0(\mathscr {O}_X)=1$ unconditional results. Note that X may be reducible, non-reduced, or non-schematic, and the ground field k is arbitrary. Building on this, the second author has treated the case of non-proper algebraic spaces over ground fields (Schröer xxx). ## 9 The Notion of Albanese Maps

Let S be a base scheme, and X be an algebraic space where the structure morphism X\rightarrow S$X\rightarrow S$ is proper, flat, of finite presentation, and cohomologically flat in degree d=0$d=0$. Then {\text {Pic}}_{X/S}^\tau ${\text {Pic}}_{X/S}^\tau $ exists as an algebraic space whose structure morphism is of finite presentation (hence quasiseparated) and locally separated, according to Theorem 2.1. We now come to the central topic of this paper, where we re-define and generalize classical notions of Albanese varieties and Albanese maps:

### Definition 8.1

An Albanese map for X is a pair (P, f) where P\rightarrow S$P\rightarrow S$ is a family of para-abelian varieties and f:X\rightarrow P$f:X\rightarrow P$ is a morphism satisfying the following condition: For each s\in S$s\in S$ the homomorphism f^*$f^*$ identifies {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{P/S}\otimes \kappa (s)${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{P/S}\otimes \kappa (s)$ with the maximal abelian subvariety of {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\otimes \kappa (s)${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}\otimes \kappa (s)$.

Now suppose that X is an algebraic space whose structure morphism X\rightarrow S$X\rightarrow S$ is proper, flat, of finite presentation and cohomologically flat in degree d=0$d=0$, with h^0(\mathscr {O}_{X_s})=1$h^0(\mathscr {O}_{X_s})=1$ for all points s\in S$s\in S$. Then {\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}${\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$ is an algebraic space endowed with a group structure whose structure morphism is of finite presentation (hence quasiseparated) and locally separated. Note that it is neither flat nor separated in general. We can formulate the main result of this paper:

### Theorem 10.2

Assumptions as above. Then G={\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$G={\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$ admits a family of maximal abelian subvarieties if and only if there is an Albanese map f:X\rightarrow P$f:X\rightarrow P$. Moreover, it is universal for morphisms to families of para-abelian varieties, and commutes with base-change.

Note that in the relative setting, the assumption is restrictive: For example, a Weierstraß equation over a discrete valuation ring R whose discriminant \Delta $\Delta $ is non-zero and belongs to \mathfrak {m}_R$\mathfrak {m}_R$ defines a family X\subset \mathbb {P}^2_R$X\subset \mathbb {P}^2_R$ of cubics where G={\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$G={\text {Pic}}^\tau _{X/S}$ does not admit a family of maximal abelian subvarieties: The generic fiber G_\eta $G_\eta $ is a one-dimensional abelian variety isomorphic to X_\eta $X_\eta $, whereas the closed fiber of G is isomorphic to the multiplicative or the additive group.

L1@P0: ANTI-AFFINE ALGEBRAIC GROUPS
L2@P0: MICHEL BRION
L3@P0: Abstract. We say that an algebraic group G over a field is antiaffine if every regular function on G is constant. We obtain a
L4@P0: classification of these groups, with applications to the structure of
L5@P0: algebraic groups in positive characteristics, and to the construction
L6@P0: of many counterexamples to Hilbert’s fourteenth problem.
L7@P0: 0. Introduction
L8@P0: We say that a group scheme G of finite type over a field k is antiaffine if O(G) = k; then G is known to be smooth, connected and
L9@P0: commutative. Examples include abelian varieties, their universal vector
L10@P0: extensions (in characteristic 0 only) and certain semi-abelian varieties.
L11@P0: The classes of anti-affine groups and of affine (or, equivalently, linear) group schemes play complementary roles in the structure of group
L12@P0: schemes over fields. Indeed, any connected group scheme G, of finite
L13@P0: type over k, has a smallest normal subgroup scheme Gant such that the
L14@P0: quotient G/Gant is affine. Moreover, Gant is anti-affine and central in G
L15@P0: (see [DG70]). Also, G has a smallest normal connected affine subgroup
L16@P0: scheme Gaff such that G/Gaff is an abelian variety (as follows from
L17@P0: Chevalley’s structure theorem, see [BLR90]). This yields the Rosenlicht decomposition: G = Gaff Gant and Gaff ∩ Gant contains (Gant)aff as
L18@P0: an algebraic subgroup of finite index (see [Ro56]).
L19@P0: Affine group schemes have been extensively investigated, but little seems to be known about their anti-affine counterparts; they only
L20@P0: appear implicitly in work of Rosenlicht and Serre (see [Ro58, Ro61,
L21@P0: Se58a]). Here we obtain some fundamental properties of anti-affine
L22@P0: groups, and reduce their structure to that of abelian varieties.
L23@P0: In Theorem 2.7, we classify anti-affine algebraic groups G over an
L24@P0: arbitrary field k with separable closure ks. In positive characteristics,
L25@P0: G is a semi-abelian variety, parametrized by a pair (A, Λ) where A is an
L26@P0: abelian variety over k, and Λ is a sublattice of A(ks), stable under the
L27@P0: action of the Galois group. The classification is a bit more complicated
L28@P0: in characteristic 0: the parameters are then triples (A, Λ, V ) where A
L29@P0: and Λ are as above, and V is a subspace of the Lie algebra of A. In
L30@P0: both cases, A is the dual of the abelian variety G/Gaff.

L34@P1: Together with the Rosenlicht decomposition, our classification yields
